pl-l4d40c2-d1e115.summary: Quotes Isidore on computing degrees: the series of kinship is divided into six degrees: son and daughter, brother and sister, are the trunk; from it branch grandson and granddaughter, first; great-grandchildren, second; great-great-grandchildren, third; and so on to the sixth.
claims: Isidore counts six degrees from the sibling trunk.

pl-l4d40c2-d1e121.summary: Notes that Isidore puts only six degrees because he does not count the trunk among the degrees.

pl-l4d40c2-d1e124.summary: Notes that others who put seven degrees count the trunk among them.

pl-l4d40c2-d1e128.summary: Explains that degrees are computed variously: some put the father in the first degree and children in the second; others call children the first degree, denying a degree between father and son, who are one flesh. Authorities forbidding to the seventh degree put the father first; those forbidding to the sixth call children the first; so the same persons are found in the sixth or seventh degree.
claims: Differences in computation explain six versus seven degrees.

pl-l4d40c2-d1e134.summary: Cites Pope Zachary's computation: I and my brother are one generation and make the first degree; my son and my brother's son the second generation and degree; and so on.

pl-l4d40c2-d1e140.summary: Concludes that between those who count six degrees and those who count seven there is no difference in meaning, only in number; the last generation, counted from the brothers, is the seventh.
claims: The two counts agree in substance.

pl-l4d40c2.summary: Explains computing degrees of kinship. Isidore counts six degrees, not counting the trunk, siblings, from grandchildren to great-great-great-grandchildren; others count seven, counting the trunk. Some put the father in the first degree and children in the second, others make children the first, denying a degree between father and son, who are one flesh; so the same persons fall in the sixth or seventh degree. Pope Zachary counts brothers as the first degree and their sons as the second; the six- and seven-degree counts agree in substance.
claims: Isidore counts six degrees; others seven, including the trunk.
Different counting methods place the same persons in different degrees.
The six- and seven-degree counts agree in substance.
